```{r sample}
R <- CODE$relation
has_col <- function(v, d = pd) v %in% names(d) && data.table::uniqueN(na.omit(d[[v]])) > 1
has_sr <- has_col("sub_round"); has_typeday <- has_col("type_day")
has_nic <- "nic" %in% names(pd) && any(!is.na(pd$nic))
has_dist <- "dist_id" %in% names(pd)

# Analysis population: diarists who are women or men, excluding live-in non-relatives (rel 9),
# who keep their own diaries but are not members of the family whose allocation is studied.
# All derived columns are created on A before any subset is taken.
A <- pd[sex %in% c("Men", "Women") & (is.na(rel) | rel != R["servant_nonrelative"])]
A[, `:=`(
  collect = water_fetch + fuel_gather,
  rural = 1L - urban,
  ownuse_rest = ownuse_goods - water_fetch - fuel_gather,
  selfcare_rest = selfcare_all - sleep,
  sector_f = factor(ifelse(urban == 1, "Urban", "Rural"), levels = c("Rural", "Urban")),
  grp = factor(fcase(female == 1 & age <= 14, "Girls 6--14", female == 1 & age <= 17, "Girls 15--17",
                     female == 1, "Women 18+", female == 0 & age <= 14, "Boys 6--14",
                     female == 0 & age <= 17, "Boys 15--17", default = "Men 18+"),
               levels = c("Girls 6--14", "Girls 15--17", "Women 18+", "Boys 6--14", "Boys 15--17", "Men 18+")),
  age_f = factor(age)
)]
A[, any_collect := as.integer(collect > 0)]
A[, dist_sec := if (has_dist) paste(dist_id, urban, sep = "_") else paste(state, urban, sep = "_")]
A[, hi := if (has_sr) as.integer(sub_round == 2) else NA_integer_]
A[, st_sr := if (has_sr) paste(state, sub_round, sep = "_") else NA_character_]
# Agricultural workers: usual status employed, 2-digit NIC 2008 division 01-03. A 5-digit code
# is reduced to its first two digits.
A[, nic2 := if (has_nic) fifelse(!is.na(nic) & nic > 99, nic %/% 1000, nic) else NA_real_]
A[, agri := if (has_nic) as.integer(employed == 1 & nic2 %in% CODE$nic_agriculture) else NA_integer_]

# Household counts among diarists (members aged 6+), added to A before any subset.
hc <- A[, .(
  h_collect = sum(collect), h_any = as.integer(any(collect > 0)),
  h_onlyf = if (any(collect > 0)) as.integer(all(female[collect > 0] == 1)) else NA_integer_,
  h_girl = as.integer(any(collect > 0 & female == 1 & age <= 17)),
  h_child = as.integer(any(collect > 0 & age <= 17)),
  n_nonemp_w = sum(female == 1 & age >= 18 & age <= 69 & employed == 0 &
                     !(pas %in% c(CODE$pas_student, CODE$pas_disabled)), na.rm = TRUE),
  n_emp_w = sum(female == 1 & age >= 18 & employed == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_girl1017 = sum(female == 1 & age >= 10 & age <= 17),
  n_boy1017 = sum(female == 0 & age >= 10 & age <= 17),
  n_men18 = sum(female == 0 & age >= 18),
  n_jmw = sum(female == 1 & married == 1 & rel == R["child_spouse"] & age >= 15 & age <= 49, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = hh_id]
A[hc, on = "hh_id", names(hc)[-1] := mget(paste0("i.", names(hc)[-1]))]

# Time accounting: ten categories that partition the 1,440-minute day.
RA <- c(collect = "Water and fuel collection", employment = "Employment and related travel",
        ownuse_rest = "Other own-use production", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic services",
        unpaid_care = "Unpaid caregiving", volunteer = "Volunteer and other unpaid work",
        learning = "Learning", free_time = "Free time", sleep = "Sleep",
        selfcare_rest = "Eating, hygiene and other self-care")
DISP <- setdiff(names(RA), "collect")
acc_gap <- A[, max(abs(rowSums(.SD) - 1440)), .SDcols = names(RA)]

# Controls and fixed effects
XC <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "i(marital_f)", "hh_size", "hh_n_under6", "hh_n_60plus")
FE_A <- c("dist_id", "dow", "sub_round")
fe_used <- function(d, v) { v <- v[v %in% names(d)]; v[vapply(v, function(x) data.table::uniqueN(na.omit(d[[x]])) > 1, logical(1))] }
fe_words <- function(v) {
  w <- c(dist_id = "district", state = "state", dist_sec = "district-by-sector", dow = "day-of-week",
         sub_round = "sub-round", st_sr = "state-by-sub-round", hh_id = "household", sib_id = "sibling-set")
  v <- unname(w[v]); if (!length(v)) return("no")
  if (length(v) == 1) v else paste(paste(v[-length(v)], collapse = ", "), "and", v[length(v)])
}
n_fsu <- uniqueN(A$fsu)
```

```{r helpers}
cell <- function(k, scale = 1, d = 1) if (is.null(k$est) || is.na(k$est)) "--" else
  paste0(.fmt(scale * k$est, d), stars(k$p), " (", .fmt(scale * k$se, d), ")")
row_df <- function(lab, vals) { d <- as.data.frame(as.list(c(unname(lab), unname(vals))), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  names(d) <- paste0("V", seq_along(d)); d }
lin2 <- function(m, a, b, s = 1) {
  if (is.null(m) || !all(c(a, b) %in% names(coef(m)))) return(list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA))
  v <- vcov(m); est <- unname(coef(m)[a] + s * coef(m)[b])
  se <- sqrt(v[a, a] + v[b, b] + 2 * s * v[a, b])
  list(est = est, se = unname(se), p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(est / unname(se))))
}
ok <- function(e) !is.null(e$est) && !is.na(e$est)
# "12.3 minutes, SE 1.1" for use inside parentheses
es <- function(e, unit = " minutes", scale = 1, d = 1) if (!ok(e)) "not estimable" else
  paste0(.fmt(scale * e$est, d), unit, ", SE ", .fmt(scale * e$se, d))
# Signed estimate with SE, no direction word (safe when the estimate may be NA)
sg <- function(e, unit = "minutes", d = 1) if (!ok(e)) "not estimable" else est_se(e, d, unit)
cse <- function(e, d = 2) if (!ok(e)) "not estimable" else paste0(.fmt(e$est, d), " (SE ", .fmt(e$se, d), ")")
ppx <- function(e) if (!ok(e)) "not estimable" else paste0(.fmt(100 * e$est, 1), " percentage points (SE ", .fmt(100 * e$se, 1), ")")
mcell <- function(r, scale = 1, d = 1) if (is.null(r) || !nrow(r) || is.na(r$est[1])) "--" else
  paste0(.fmt(scale * r$est[1], d), " (", .fmt(scale * r$se[1], d), ")")
safe_mean <- function(d, y, weight = "weight") {
  if (!nrow(d) || all(is.na(d[[y]])) || sum(d[[weight]], na.rm = TRUE) <= 0) return(data.frame(est = NA, se = NA, n = 0))
  v <- d[[y]][!is.na(d[[y]])]
  if (all(v == v[1])) return(data.frame(est = v[1], se = 0, n = length(v)))   # constant (e.g. nobody collects)
  tryCatch(est_mean(d, y, weight = weight), error = function(e) data.frame(est = NA, se = NA, n = nrow(d)))
}
cap1 <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substring(x, 2))
ivF <- function(m) if (is.null(m)) NA_real_ else tryCatch(unname(fitstat(m, "ivwald1")[[1]]$stat), error = function(e) NA_real_)
```

```{r partA}
# ---- Part A: who collects ----------------------------------------------------------
gm <- function(d, y) safe_mean(d, y)
pa_vars <- c("any_water_fetch", "water_fetch", "any_fuel_gather", "fuel_gather", "collect")
burden <- rbindlist(lapply(c("Rural", "Urban", "All"), function(s) {
  d0 <- if (s == "All") A else A[sector_f == s]
  rbindlist(lapply(levels(A$grp), function(g) {
    d <- d0[grp == g]
    data.table(sector = s, group = g, n = nrow(d),
               p_w = list(gm(d, "any_water_fetch")), m_w = list(gm(d, "water_fetch")),
               p_f = list(gm(d, "any_fuel_gather")), m_f = list(gm(d, "fuel_gather")),
               m_c = list(gm(d, "collect")), m_cd = list(gm(d[collect > 0], "collect")))
  }))
}))
bget <- function(s, g, v) { r <- burden[sector == s & group == g][[v]]; if (!length(r)) list(est = NA, se = NA) else as.list(r[[1]][1, c("est", "se")]) }
pw_rw <- bget("Rural", "Women 18+", "p_w"); pw_rm <- bget("Rural", "Men 18+", "p_w")
pf_rw <- bget("Rural", "Women 18+", "p_f"); pf_rm <- bget("Rural", "Men 18+", "p_f")
pw_uw <- bget("Urban", "Women 18+", "p_w"); pw_um <- bget("Urban", "Men 18+", "p_w")
mc_rw <- bget("Rural", "Women 18+", "m_c"); mc_rm <- bget("Rural", "Men 18+", "m_c")
mcd_rw <- bget("Rural", "Women 18+", "m_cd"); mcd_rm <- bget("Rural", "Men 18+", "m_cd")
pw_rg <- bget("Rural", "Girls 15--17", "p_w"); pw_rb <- bget("Rural", "Boys 15--17", "p_w")
pw_rg6 <- bget("Rural", "Girls 6--14", "p_w"); pw_rb6 <- bget("Rural", "Boys 6--14", "p_w")
# Adult participation gaps (women minus men), rural
A18r <- A[age >= 18 & rural == 1]
g_pw <- est_gap(A18r, "any_water_fetch", "female", 0, 1)
g_pf <- est_gap(A18r, "any_fuel_gather", "female", 0, 1)
g_mc <- est_gap(A18r, "collect", "female", 0, 1)

# Share of all collection minutes done by female members (and by girls under 18):
# a weighted mean of the female indicator with weights = survey weight x minutes.
A[, `:=`(w_c = weight * collect, w_w = weight * water_fetch, w_f = weight * fuel_gather,
         girl18 = as.integer(female == 1 & age <= 17), child18 = as.integer(age <= 17))]
fsh <- function(d, wv, y = "female") { d <- d[get(wv) > 0]; if (!nrow(d)) return(list(est = NA, se = NA)) else as.list(safe_mean(d, y, wv)[1, c("est", "se")]) }
sh_c <- fsh(A, "w_c"); sh_w <- fsh(A, "w_w"); sh_f <- fsh(A, "w_f")
sh_c_r <- fsh(A[rural == 1], "w_c"); sh_c_u <- fsh(A[rural == 0], "w_c")
sh_girl <- fsh(A, "w_c", "girl18"); sh_child <- fsh(A, "w_c", "child18")

# Household level: among households in which any diarist collected, only female members collected
H <- unique(A[, .(hh_id, fsu, rural, h_any, h_onlyf, h_girl, h_child, h_collect,
                  weight = ave(weight, hh_id, FUN = mean))], by = "hh_id")
HC <- H[h_any == 1]
hh_onlyf <- as.list(safe_mean(HC, "h_onlyf")[1, c("est", "se")])
hh_onlyf_r <- as.list(safe_mean(HC[rural == 1], "h_onlyf")[1, c("est", "se")])
hh_onlyf_u <- as.list(safe_mean(HC[rural == 0], "h_onlyf")[1, c("est", "se")])
hh_girl <- as.list(safe_mean(HC, "h_girl")[1, c("est", "se")])
hh_share_any <- as.list(safe_mean(H, "h_any")[1, c("est", "se")])
hh_share_any_r <- as.list(safe_mean(H[rural == 1], "h_any")[1, c("est", "se")])
hh_min <- as.list(safe_mean(HC, "h_collect")[1, c("est", "se")])
fem_major <- isTRUE(sh_c$est > 0.5)
onlyf_major <- isTRUE(hh_onlyf$est > 0.5)
```

```{r partB}
# ---- Part B1: within-household gap among members 10+ -------------------------------
HB <- A[age >= 10]
HB[, mix := uniqueN(female) == 2, by = hh_id]
HB <- HB[mix == TRUE]
b_y <- c(collect = "Water and fuel collection (minutes)", water_fetch = "Fetching water (minutes)",
         fuel_gather = "Gathering fuel (minutes)", any_collect = "Any collection (pp)",
         any_water_fetch = "Any water fetching (pp)", any_fuel_gather = "Any fuel gathering (pp)")
f_hh <- function(y, d = HB, rhs = "female") reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", rhs, "+", ctrl(d, c("i(age_band)", "i(dow_f)")), "| hh_id")), d)
mHH <- setNames(lapply(names(b_y), f_hh), names(b_y))
mHR <- setNames(lapply(names(b_y), f_hh, rhs = "female + female:urban"), names(b_y))
mCS <- setNames(lapply(names(b_y), function(y) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ female +", ctrl(HB, c(XC, "urban")), fe(HB, FE_A))), HB)), names(b_y))
kh <- function(y, ml = mHH, t = "female") coef_of(ml[[y]], t)
k_hh <- kh("collect"); k_hh_w <- kh("water_fetch"); k_hh_f <- kh("fuel_gather"); k_hh_any <- kh("any_collect")
k_hh_urb <- kh("collect", mHR, "female:urban"); k_hh_rur <- kh("collect", mHR)
k_cs <- kh("collect", mCS)
n_hh_B <- uniqueN(HB$hh_id)
mean_male_B <- wmean(HB[female == 0]$collect, HB[female == 0]$weight)

# ---- Part B2: women's roles within the household ---------------------------------
W <- A[female == 1 & age >= 15 & !is.na(rel)]
W[, role := factor(fcase(rel == R["spouse"], "Head's spouse", rel == R["head"], "Female head",
                         rel == R["child_spouse"], "Daughter-in-law",
                         rel %in% R[c("married_child", "unmarried_child")], "Daughter",
                         rel == R["parent_or_inlaw"], "Head's mother or mother-in-law",
                         default = "Other female relative"),
                   levels = c("Head's spouse", "Female head", "Daughter-in-law", "Daughter",
                              "Head's mother or mother-in-law", "Other female relative"))]
W[, nrole := uniqueN(role), by = hh_id]
WB <- W[nrole >= 2]
roles <- setdiff(levels(W$role), "Head's spouse")
f_role <- function(y, age = FALSE) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ i(role, ref = \"Head's spouse\")",
                                                        if (age) paste("+", ctrl(WB, c("i(age_band)", "i(dow_f)"))) else "", "| hh_id")), WB)
mR0 <- f_role("collect"); mR1 <- f_role("collect", TRUE); mRa <- f_role("any_collect", TRUE)
kr <- function(m, r) coef_of(m, paste0("role::", r))
k_dil <- kr(mR1, "Daughter-in-law"); k_dau <- kr(mR1, "Daughter")
k_dil0 <- kr(mR0, "Daughter-in-law"); k_dau0 <- kr(mR0, "Daughter")
k_dil_dau <- lin2(mR1, "role::Daughter-in-law", "role::Daughter", -1)
n_hh_dil_dau <- W[, any(role == "Daughter-in-law") & any(role == "Daughter"), by = hh_id][V1 == TRUE, .N]
role_means <- W[, .(m = wmean(collect, weight), p = wmean(any_collect, weight), n = .N), by = role][order(role)]

# ---- Part B3: does another woman or a girl take the load off the main woman? -------
# Focal woman: married, 20-49, the head or head's spouse in a household with no junior married
# woman of childbearing age, or the unique daughter-in-law. (A head-level woman who lives with a
# married daughter-in-law is usually the older generation.)
M <- A[female == 1 & married == 1 & age >= 20 & age <= 49 &
         ((rel %in% R[c("head", "spouse")] & n_jmw == 0) | (rel == R["child_spouse"] & n_jmw == 1))]
M[, `:=`(
  own_nonemp = as.integer(age <= 69 & employed == 0 & !(pas %in% c(CODE$pas_student, CODE$pas_disabled))),
  others_collect = h_collect - collect
)]
M[, `:=`(oth_nonemp = as.integer(n_nonemp_w - own_nonemp > 0),
         oth_emp_w = n_emp_w - employed,
         girl1017 = as.integer(n_girl1017 > 0), boy1017 = as.integer(n_boy1017 > 0))]
xm <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "urban", "n_men18", "oth_emp_w", "hh_n_under6", "hh_n_6_14", "hh_n_60plus", "proxy_report")
f_mo <- function(y, d = M) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ oth_nonemp + girl1017 + boy1017 +", ctrl(d, xm), fe(d, FE_A))), d)
mo_y <- c(collect = "Her collection (minutes)", any_collect = "Her participation (pp)", others_collect = "Others' collection (minutes)")
mMo <- setNames(lapply(names(mo_y), f_mo), names(mo_y))
mMoR <- f_mo("collect", M[rural == 1])
k_mo_w <- coef_of(mMo$collect, "oth_nonemp"); k_mo_g <- coef_of(mMo$collect, "girl1017"); k_mo_b <- coef_of(mMo$collect, "boy1017")
k_mo_gb <- lin2(mMo$collect, "girl1017", "boy1017", -1)
k_mo_g_oth <- coef_of(mMo$others_collect, "girl1017"); k_mo_w_oth <- coef_of(mMo$others_collect, "oth_nonemp")
k_mo_g_r <- coef_of(mMoR, "girl1017"); k_mo_w_r <- coef_of(mMoR, "oth_nonemp")
mean_M <- wmean(M$collect, M$weight)
```

```{r partC}
# ---- Part C: seasonality as a shifter of collection need --------------------------
A15 <- A[age >= 15]; G <- A[female == 1 & age >= 10 & age <= 17]
A15r <- A15[rural == 1]
FE_R <- c("dist_id", "dow")                       # rural reduced form: within district
FE_IV <- c("dist_sec", "sub_round", "dow")        # 2SLS: district-by-sector and quarter FE
XC_G <- c("i(age_f)", "hh_size", "hh_n_under6", "hh_n_60plus", "i(head_edu_tier)")

# Quarter profile of collection in rural areas (relative to sub-round 1)
prof_grp <- list("Women 15+" = A15r[female == 1], "Men 15+" = A15r[female == 0], "Girls 10--17" = G[rural == 1])
prof <- rbindlist(lapply(names(prof_grp), function(g) {
  d <- prof_grp[[g]]
  m <- reg(as.formula(paste("collect ~ i(sub_round, ref = 1) +", ctrl(d, if (g == "Girls 10--17") XC_G else XC), fe(d, FE_R))), d)
  rbindlist(lapply(2:4, function(q) { k <- coef_of(m, paste0("sub_round::", q)); data.table(group = g, q = q, est = k$est, se = k$se) }))
}))
q_means <- if (has_sr) A15r[female == 1, .(m = wmean(collect, weight)), by = sub_round][order(sub_round)] else data.table(sub_round = NA, m = NA)
peak_q <- if (all(is.na(q_means$m))) NA else q_means$sub_round[which.max(q_means$m)]

# Reduced form, rural: each category on the high-need quarter (sub-round 2), within district.
rf <- function(y, d) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ hi +", ctrl(d, XC), fe(d, FE_R))), d)
rfG <- function(y, d) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ hi +", ctrl(d, XC_G), fe(d, FE_R))), d)
RFw <- setNames(lapply(names(RA), rf, d = A15r[female == 1]), names(RA))
RFm <- setNames(lapply(names(RA), rf, d = A15r[female == 0]), names(RA))
RFg <- setNames(lapply(names(RA), rfG, d = G[rural == 1]), names(RA))
krf <- function(ml, y) coef_of(ml[[y]], "hi")
rf_w <- krf(RFw, "collect"); rf_m <- krf(RFm, "collect"); rf_g <- krf(RFg, "collect")
rf_w_emp <- krf(RFw, "employment"); rf_m_emp <- krf(RFm, "employment")
rf_sum_w <- sum(sapply(names(RA), function(y) krf(RFw, y)$est), na.rm = TRUE)
base_rw <- if (has_sr) wmean(A15r[female == 1 & hi == 0]$collect, A15r[female == 1 & hi == 0]$weight) else NA
rf_up_w <- is_pos(rf_w); rf_up_m <- is_pos(rf_m)

# 2SLS: displaced minutes per minute of collection. Instruments: quarter x rural, with
# district-by-sector and quarter fixed effects (so common seasonal shocks are differenced out).
INST <- "collect ~ i(sub_round, rural, ref = 1)"
iv <- function(y, d, xv = XC, fev = FE_IV, w = TRUE) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(y, "~", ctrl(d, xv), fe(d, fev), "|", INST))
  if (w) reg(f, d) else tryCatch(feols(f, d, cluster = ~fsu), error = function(e) NULL)
}
IVw <- setNames(lapply(DISP, iv, d = A15[female == 1]), DISP)
IVm <- setNames(lapply(DISP, iv, d = A15[female == 0]), DISP)
IVg <- setNames(lapply(DISP, iv, d = G, xv = XC_G), DISP)
kiv <- function(ml, y) coef_of(ml[[y]], "fit_collect")
F_w <- ivF(IVw$employment); F_m <- ivF(IVm$employment); F_g <- ivF(IVg$learning)
strong_w <- isTRUE(F_w >= 10); strong_m <- isTRUE(F_m >= 10); strong_g <- isTRUE(F_g >= 10)
lmmp_w <- isTRUE(F_w >= 104.7)
iv_sum <- function(ml) sum(sapply(DISP, function(y) kiv(ml, y)$est), na.rm = TRUE)
ivs_w <- iv_sum(IVw); ivs_m <- iv_sum(IVm)
iv_est_w <- sapply(DISP, function(y) kiv(IVw, y)$est)
top_disp_w <- if (all(is.na(iv_est_w))) NA_character_ else names(which.min(iv_est_w))
top2_disp_w <- if (sum(!is.na(iv_est_w)) < 2) NA_character_ else names(sort(iv_est_w))[2]
k_iv_w_emp <- kiv(IVw, "employment"); k_iv_w_dom <- kiv(IVw, "unpaid_domestic"); k_iv_w_free <- kiv(IVw, "free_time")
k_iv_w_sleep <- kiv(IVw, "sleep"); k_iv_w_care <- kiv(IVw, "unpaid_care")
k_iv_m_emp <- kiv(IVm, "employment"); k_iv_g_learn <- kiv(IVg, "learning"); k_iv_g_free <- kiv(IVg, "free_time")
k_iv_g_sleep <- kiv(IVg, "sleep")
# First-stage coefficient on quarter 2 x rural (women)
fs_w <- if (is.null(IVw$employment)) list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA) else coef_of(summary(IVw$employment, stage = 1), "sub_round::2:rural")

# Threat: does men's paid work move with rural quarters? Joint test of quarter x rural in a
# reduced form for men's employment (same FE as the 2SLS).
rf_threat <- function(d, y = "employment") {
  m <- reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ i(sub_round, rural, ref = 1) +", ctrl(d, XC), fe(d, FE_IV))), d)
  if (is.null(m)) return(list(p = NA, m = NULL))
  w <- tryCatch(wald(m, keep = "sub_round::", print = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
  list(p = if (is.null(w)) NA else unname(w$p), m = m)
}
thr_m <- rf_threat(A15[female == 0]); thr_w <- rf_threat(A15[female == 1])
paid_seasonal <- isTRUE(thr_m$p < 0.05) || isTRUE(thr_w$p < 0.05)

# Robustness of women's 2SLS
rb_y <- c("employment", "unpaid_domestic", "free_time", "sleep")
W15 <- A15[female == 1]
specs <- list(
  base = list(lab = "Baseline", f = function(y) IVw[[y]]),
  pas  = list(lab = "Adding usual principal activity status", f = function(y) iv(y, W15, c(XC, "i(pas_group)"))),
  noag = list(lab = "Excluding agricultural workers (NIC 01--03)", f = function(y) if (has_nic) iv(y, W15[agri == 0]) else NULL),
  nemp = list(lab = "Women not employed (usual status)", f = function(y) iv(y, W15[employed == 0])),
  stq  = list(lab = "State-by-quarter fixed effects", f = function(y) iv(y, W15, fev = c("dist_sec", "st_sr", "dow"))),
  self = list(lab = "Self-reported diaries", f = function(y) iv(y, W15[proxy_report == 0])),
  unw  = list(lab = "Unweighted", f = function(y) iv(y, W15, w = FALSE)))
if (has_typeday) specs$normal <- list(lab = "Normal routine days only", f = function(y) iv(y, W15[type_day == CODE$type_of_day["normal"]]))
RB <- lapply(specs, function(s) {
  ms <- lapply(setNames(rb_y, rb_y), s$f)
  list(k = lapply(ms, coef_of, "fit_collect"), F = ivF(ms$employment),
       n = if (is.null(ms$employment)) NA else nobs(ms$employment))
})
rb_emp_noag <- RB$noag$k$employment; rb_emp_pas <- RB$pas$k$employment; rb_emp_nemp <- RB$nemp$k$employment
same_sign <- function(e, b) isTRUE(ok(e) && ok(b) && sign(e$est) == sign(b$est))
n_rb_same_emp <- sum(sapply(setdiff(names(RB), "base"), function(s) same_sign(RB[[s]]$k$employment, k_iv_w_emp)))
n_rb_est <- sum(sapply(setdiff(names(RB), "base"), function(s) ok(RB[[s]]$k$employment)))
```

```{r partD}
# ---- Girls' schooling time: sibling comparison -------------------------------------
K <- A[age >= 10 & age <= 17 & rel %in% R[c("unmarried_child", "grandchild")] &
         (is.na(marital) | marital == CODE$marital["never_married"])]
K[, `:=`(sib_id = paste(hh_id, rel), girl = female)]
K[, mixed := uniqueN(girl) == 2, by = sib_id]
S <- K[mixed == TRUE]
f_sib <- function(y, rhs = "girl", d = S) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", rhs, "+ i(age_f) | sib_id")), d)
sib_y <- c(collect = "Water and fuel collection", any_collect = "Any collection (pp)", learning = "Learning",
           unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic services", free_time = "Free time")
mS <- setNames(lapply(names(sib_y), f_sib), names(sib_y))
mSq <- setNames(lapply(names(sib_y), f_sib, rhs = "girl + girl:hi"), names(sib_y))
mSr <- setNames(lapply(names(sib_y), f_sib, rhs = "girl + girl:rural"), names(sib_y))
k_s_c <- coef_of(mS$collect, "girl"); k_s_l <- coef_of(mS$learning, "girl"); k_s_a <- coef_of(mS$any_collect, "girl")
k_s_cq <- coef_of(mSq$collect, "girl:hi"); k_s_lq <- coef_of(mSq$learning, "girl:hi")
k_s_cr <- coef_of(mSr$collect, "girl:rural")
n_sets <- uniqueN(S$sib_id)
girls_more <- is_pos(k_s_c)
```

\begin{abstract}
Fetching water and gathering fuel are physically demanding forms of unpaid work in rural India, widely described as the work of women and girls. I use the Time Use Survey 2024, which records a full-day diary for every household member aged six and above, to measure who carries this burden, how it is divided within households, and what it costs in other activities when the need for it rises. In rural areas, `r pctx(pw_rw$est)` of women aged 18 and above fetched water on the diary day, compared with `r pctx(pw_rm$est)` of men, and `r pctx(pf_rw$est)` of women gathered fuel, compared with `r pctx(pf_rm$est)` of men. Female members do `r pctx(sh_c$est)` of all collection minutes. Among households in which anyone collected, only female members did so in `r pctx(hh_onlyf$est)`. Within the same household, female members aged 10 and above spend `r diff_txt(k_hh)` on collection than male members. `r iff(is_pos(k_dil_dau), "Daughters-in-law collect more than daughters of the same age in the same household.", "Daughters-in-law and daughters of the same age in the same household do not differ significantly in collection time.")` Using the survey quarter as a shifter of collection need within districts, rural women's collection is `r diff_txt(rf_w, "higher", "lower")` in the second sub-round than in other quarters. `r iff(strong_w && !is.na(top_disp_w), paste0("Instrumenting collection with quarter by sector variation, the largest offsetting change in women's time, as a point estimate, is in ", tolower(RA[top_disp_w]), "."), "Quarter by sector variation is too weak to support a two-stage estimate of what collection displaces, so I report the reduced form.")` `r iff(paid_seasonal, "Paid work also varies with the rural quarter, so these estimates mix the time cost of collection with agricultural seasonality; I report checks that hold usual activity status fixed or drop agricultural workers.", "Paid work does not vary significantly with the rural quarter, which removes the most direct threat to reading the seasonal estimates as the time cost of collection.")` `r iff(fem_major, "The time that reliable household water connections could release is therefore concentrated on women and girls.", "The time that reliable household water connections could release is shared between women and men.")`
\keywords{water collection, firewood, time use, intrahousehold allocation, seasonality, gender, India}
\jel{J16, J22, O13, Q25, D13}
\end{abstract}

\newpage

# Introduction

In much of rural India, the water a household drinks, cooks and washes with is carried home from a well, a hand pump, a public tap or a pond, and much of the fuel it cooks with is gathered from fields and forests. The national programme to provide a functional tap connection to every rural household, the Jal Jeevan Mission launched in 2019 [@mojs2019jjm], rests in part on the argument that this work takes time, that the time is mostly women's and girls', and that it competes with paid work, schooling and rest. The same argument has been made for decades in the development literature [@agarwal1986cold; @ray2007women; @blackden2006gender; @sorenson2011safe]. Its quantitative basis, however, comes mostly from household surveys that ask who usually fetches water and how long a trip takes [@whounicef2017progress; @graham2016analysis], from small area studies, or from evaluations of particular projects, rather than from complete diaries for all household members in a national sample.

This paper uses the Time Use Survey 2024 [@nso2025tus] to measure water and fuel collection directly. The survey records a 24-hour diary, coded to the International Classification of Activities for Time-Use Statistics [@un2016icatus], for every household member aged six and above, in a national sample of `r fn(V$n_households)` households. The ICATUS classification gives fetching water (code 242) and gathering firewood and other natural fuel (code 241) their own codes in the division for production of goods for own final use. Because every member of a household keeps a diary, the data show not only how much collection women and men do on average but how the work is divided among the members of a single household on the same day.

The paper has three parts. The first is descriptive: who collects, how much, and how concentrated the work is on women and girls, by age, sex and sector, and at the household level. The second studies intrahousehold allocation. Using household fixed effects, I compare female and male members aged 10 and above in the same household, women in different positions in the household (the head's spouse, a daughter-in-law, a daughter), and the main married woman's own collection time in households with and without another non-employed adult woman or an adolescent girl. The third uses seasonality. The survey was fielded over four quarters (sub-rounds), with sample first-stage units spread evenly across them, so within a district the quarter in which a household was surveyed shifts the need for collection. I estimate how much collection rises in the quarter of highest expected need and what other activities fall when it does, using the 1,440-minute identity to account for the whole day. Because sub-round is a shifter of need and not a randomised instrument, and because agricultural seasonality moves paid work in the same quarters, I state the threats to this design explicitly and report checks that hold usual activity status fixed, drop agricultural workers and add state-by-quarter fixed effects. A short final section compares sisters and brothers aged 10 to 17 in the same household on collection and learning time.

The headline numbers are these. In rural India, `r pct(pw_rw$est)` of women aged 18 and above fetched water on the diary day, against `r pct(pw_rm$est)` of men; `r pct(pf_rw$est)` of women and `r pct(pf_rm$est)` of men gathered fuel. Female members, adults and girls together, account for `r pct(sh_c$est)` of all minutes spent collecting water and fuel, and girls under 18 alone for `r pct(sh_girl$est)`. `r iff(onlyf_major, paste0("In ", pct(hh_onlyf$est), " of households in which anyone collected, every member who collected was female."), paste0("In ", pct(hh_onlyf$est), " of households in which anyone collected, every member who collected was female; in the rest at least one male member also collected."))` Within households, female members aged 10 and above spend `r diff_txt(k_hh)` collecting water and fuel than male members of the same household, compared with a mean of `r f1(mean_male_B)` minutes for male members. `r iff(is_pos(k_dil_dau), paste0("A daughter-in-law spends ", diff_txt(k_dil_dau), " on collection than a daughter of the same age in the same household."), paste0("The difference between a daughter-in-law and a daughter of the same age in the same household is ", sg(k_dil_dau), ", which is not significantly positive."))` In the seasonal analysis, rural women's collection in the second sub-round is `r diff_txt(rf_w, "higher", "lower")` than in the other quarters of the same district, from a base of `r f1(base_rw)` minutes. `r iff(strong_w, paste0("The first stage of the two-stage estimate is strong (F = ", f1(F_w), ")."), paste0("The first stage of the two-stage estimate is weak (F = ", f1(F_w), "), so I rely on the reduced form."))`

The paper contributes to three literatures. The first measures the time burden of water and fuel collection and its distribution by sex and age [@sorenson2011safe; @graham2016analysis; @whittington1990calculating; @gross2018women]. This paper adds complete diaries for every household member in a national sample, which allows the burden to be measured on the same footing as all other activities and divided among the members of one household. The second asks whether infrastructure that reduces collection time changes women's work and children's schooling [@ilahi2000public; @koolwal2013access; @devoto2012happiness; @meeks2017water; @nauges2017water]. That literature typically observes infrastructure and a few outcomes. Here, the full-day identity shows all the activities that adjust when collection need varies, including sleep and free time, which household surveys do not record. The third studies how households allocate work among their members [@becker1965theory; @chiappori1992collective; @agarwal1997bargaining; @udry1996gender]. Collection is a task for which household needs are shared and the allocation is visible, so it is a clean case in which to observe how position in the household, age and sex determine who works.

Section \ref{sec:lit} reviews the literature. Section \ref{sec:data} describes the data. Section \ref{sec:burden} reports the descriptive burden, Section \ref{sec:alloc} the intrahousehold allocation, and Section \ref{sec:season} the seasonal analysis. Section \ref{sec:girls} compares sisters and brothers. Section \ref{sec:disc} discusses interpretation, policy and limitations, and Section \ref{sec:conc} concludes.

# Related literature {#sec:lit}

## Water and fuel collection as women's and girls' work

That fetching water is mainly the work of women and girls is one of the most consistent findings in development research. @sorenson2011safe review household survey evidence from a large number of low- and middle-income countries and show that adult women are the members most often responsible for fetching water, that girls are more often responsible than boys, and that the burden carries health risks, from the physical strain of carrying heavy loads to injuries and assault on the way. @graham2016analysis analyse household surveys from 24 countries in sub-Saharan Africa and estimate the share of households that rely on water collected off the premises, the share of that work done by women and by children, and the gap between girls and boys. The joint monitoring reports of WHO and UNICEF record, for every country, the share of the population whose drinking water source is on the premises or within a round trip of 30 minutes [@whounicef2017progress]. @ray2007women reviews the research and policy debates on women and water, including the gap between the emphasis on women's time in policy statements and the limited measurement of it.

Fuel collection has been studied mainly through the lens of deforestation. @agarwal1986cold describes the woodfuel crisis in South Asia and elsewhere, and argues that its costs fall disproportionately on women, who gather most of the fuel and do most of the cooking. In the hills of Nepal, @kumar1988consequences find that deforestation increased the time women spent collecting fuelwood, with consequences for agricultural production and nutrition. @cooke1998intrahousehold studies how Nepali households reallocate labour among members when fuelwood and fodder become scarce, and @amacher1996household model the choice between buying fuelwood and collecting it. @baland2010environmental study the determinants of firewood collection in rural Nepal and its relation to household living standards, and @cooke2008fuelwood review the household evidence on fuelwood, forests and community management. For Africa, @blackden2006gender assemble time-use evidence showing that water and fuel collection are a central part of women's work burden and of their time poverty, a theme taken up by @bardasi2010working for Guinea.

In India, the official time-use reports document large gender gaps in unpaid work [@nso2020tus; @nso2025tus], and @hirway2011understanding show how time-use statistics reveal women's work that labour force surveys miss, including work in collection and other production for own use. National reports do not, however, divide collection among household members or relate it to other activities within a household.

## Infrastructure and the reallocation of time

A second strand asks what happens when collection becomes easier. @ilahi2000public show for rural Pakistan that women in communities with better water infrastructure spend less time collecting water and more time in market work. @koolwal2013access use surveys from several countries and find that better access to water reduces the time women spend collecting it, but find little evidence of a corresponding rise in women's paid work; in some countries the time savings are associated with better schooling outcomes for children. @meeks2017water studies rural water infrastructure in the Kyrgyz Republic and finds that the time saved from water collection was reallocated to other activities. @gross2018women measure the time women in rural Benin spend walking to and waiting at water points and estimate its value. Earlier, @whittington1990calculating used households' choices among water sources at different distances to value the time spent collecting water in Kenya, and @kremer2011spring used similar revealed-preference reasoning for the protection of springs in rural Kenya.

A striking result is that of @devoto2012happiness. In a randomised evaluation in urban Morocco, they found that households that obtained a piped connection did not experience better health but did gain time, which went mainly to leisure and social activities, and reported higher well-being. The result implies that the value of time saved from collection need not appear in earnings, and that outcomes such as rest and free time matter. Health effects of piped water are a separate literature [@jalan2003does; @galiani2005water], as are its effects on schooling: @zhang2016long find that a rural drinking water programme in China raised educational attainment, and @nauges2017water find in Ghana that longer water hauling times are associated with lower school attendance of girls. When public supply is unreliable, households bear coping costs [@pattanayak2005coping].

Related evidence comes from other infrastructure that affects household production. @dinkelman2011electrification finds that rural electrification in South Africa raised women's employment, plausibly by releasing time from home production, and @grogan2013rural find related effects in Nicaragua. @dinkelman2022time argue that the time women spend in home production, including water and fuel collection, is central to understanding gender differences in work during structural transformation. The literature on improved cookstoves and clean fuels finds that adoption and sustained use are far from automatic [@mobarak2012low; @hanna2016smoke], and in India the uptake and continued use of LPG under the Ujjwala programme have been uneven [@gould2018lpg; @kar2019ujjwala], so that firewood collection remains common.

## Intrahousehold allocation and the position of women

Who in the household does a given task depends on the household's production technology, on the members' opportunity costs and on their bargaining power and social norms. Models of household time allocation in the tradition of @becker1965theory emphasise comparative advantage; collective models [@chiappori1992collective; @lundberg1993separate] allow the allocation to depend on who has power. @agarwal1997bargaining argues that bargaining in South Asian households is shaped by social norms and by members' positions outside the household, and @udry1996gender shows that the allocation of inputs across household members' plots in Burkina Faso is not efficient, which is inconsistent with a unitary model. In patrilocal households, a daughter-in-law's position differs from a daughter's: she has married in, typically has less say, and may be assigned the heaviest tasks [@jayachandran2015roots]. Water and fuel collection is a task whose output is shared by the household and whose allocation is directly observable in diaries, so it offers a simple test of how position, age and sex shape who works.

## Children's work and schooling

Children's domestic work, of which water collection is a large part in many countries, is often omitted from measures of child labour even though it competes with school [@edmonds2008child]. @assaad2010effect show for Egypt that girls' domestic work reduces their schooling. Evidence that water collection in particular reduces girls' school attendance comes from @nauges2017water and, through infrastructure, from @koolwal2013access and @zhang2016long. A companion paper that uses the same survey studies the full allocation of time between sisters and brothers; here I report only the collection and learning margins.

## Seasonality

Rural work burdens are seasonal. @chambers1981seasonal document how the seasons concentrate work, illness and food shortage in particular months of the year in rural areas. Seasonal income fluctuations shape consumption and saving [@paxson1993consumption] and migration [@bryan2014underinvestment]. For collection, the season matters directly: in the dry months before the monsoon, nearby sources dry up and women must walk further or wait longer for water. For identification, seasonality is a double-edged tool. It shifts collection need, but it also shifts the demand for agricultural labour. I therefore use it with district fixed effects and urban areas as a comparison, and test whether paid work also moves with the season.

# Data {#sec:data}

## The Time Use Survey 2024

The Time Use Survey 2024 was conducted by the National Statistics Office from January to December 2024 [@nso2025tus]. Every household member aged six and above reports the activities of the 24 hours from 4 a.m. on the day before the interview, in 30-minute slots, with activities coded at three digits to ICATUS 2016 [@un2016icatus]. Where more than one activity is recorded in a slot, one is flagged as the major activity. I use every record in the file (`r fn(V$n_rows)` records, `r fn(V$n_diarists)` diaries in `r fn(V$n_households)` households and `r fn(V$n_fsu)` first-stage units), with no sampling of records. Minutes are computed from major activities only; `r pct(V$share_diaries_1440)` of diaries sum exactly to 1,440 minutes. All estimates use the survey weights.

`r data_disclosure(V)` The household questionnaire would also have recorded the household's primary source of energy for cooking. Without it, I cannot condition on whether the household cooks with firewood or has a piped water connection, and district fixed effects stand in for local infrastructure. This is the main limitation of the paper and I return to it in Section \ref{sec:disc}.

## Outcomes

The two outcomes are minutes per day in fetching water (ICATUS 242) and in gathering firewood and other natural products used as fuel (ICATUS 241), and indicators for any such minutes on the diary day. I call their sum "collection". Both codes belong to division 2 of ICATUS, production of goods for own final use. Travel related to own-use production is coded separately (code 250), so time spent walking to a water source may be recorded either as part of fetching water or as travel, depending on how the respondent and the enumerator recorded it; collection minutes are therefore a lower bound on the time cost if some walking time is coded as travel.

For the time accounting I divide the day into ten categories that partition the 1,440 minutes: collection; employment and related travel (division 1); other production for own use (division 2 less collection); unpaid domestic services (division 3); unpaid caregiving (division 4); volunteer and other unpaid work (division 5); learning (division 6); free time (divisions 7 and 8: socialising, community participation, religious practice, culture, leisure, mass media and sports); sleep; and eating, hygiene and other self-care (the rest of division 9). `r iff(acc_gap < 1e-6, "In the analysis sample the ten categories sum to exactly 1,440 minutes in every diary.", paste0("In the analysis sample the ten categories sum to 1,440 minutes in every diary up to ", f1(acc_gap), " minutes."))`

## Samples and variables

The analysis population is the `r fn(nrow(A))` diarists who are women or men (`r fn(nrow(pd) - nrow(A))` diaries of transgender persons and of live-in non-relatives, who include domestic workers, are excluded). I group them into girls and boys aged 6 to 14 and 15 to 17, women and men aged 18 and above, and rural and urban sectors. Household composition is counted from the full roster. The roster records each member's relationship to the head, sex, age, marital status, education and usual principal activity status. I identify a woman's position in the household from her relationship to the head: the head's spouse, a female head, a daughter-in-law (spouse of a married child), a daughter (married or unmarried child), the head's mother or mother-in-law, or another relative.

For the seasonal analysis I use the sub-round in which each first-stage unit was surveyed. `r iff(has_sr, "The file records the sub-round, a quarter of the survey year.", "The panel used here does not record the sub-round, so the seasonal analysis is not estimable.")` The 2024 data dictionary does not state the months each sub-round covers. In the 2019 round, the design document divided the survey year into four sub-rounds of three months each, January to March, April to June, July to September and October to December, with an equal number of sample first-stage units allotted to each [@nso2020tus]. If the 2024 round follows the same calendar, which its January to December reference period is consistent with but which the file does not confirm, sub-round 2 covers April to June, the hot, dry months before the monsoon reaches most of India. I designate sub-round 2 as the quarter of high collection need on this prior ground, and I report the estimates for every quarter so that the designation can be judged against the data.

Agricultural workers are persons whose usual principal activity status is a form of employment and whose two-digit industry code (National Industrial Classification 2008) is in divisions 01 to 03, agriculture, forestry and fishing. `r iff(has_nic, "The roster records the industry code.", "The panel used here does not carry the industry code, so the check that drops agricultural workers is not estimable.")`

# Who collects {#sec:burden}

```{r tab-burden}
bt <- rbindlist(lapply(c("Rural", "Urban", "All"), function(s) {
  rbind(row_df(paste0("\\textit{", s, "}"), rep("", 6)),
        rbindlist(lapply(levels(A$grp), function(g) {
          r <- burden[sector == s & group == g]
          row_df(paste0("\\quad ", g), c(mcell(r$p_w[[1]], 100), mcell(r$m_w[[1]]), mcell(r$p_f[[1]], 100),
                                         mcell(r$m_f[[1]]), mcell(r$m_cd[[1]]), fn(r$n)))
        })))
}))
names(bt) <- c("", "Water: any (\\%)", "Water: minutes", "Fuel: any (\\%)", "Fuel: minutes", "Minutes if collected", "N")
tab(bt, caption = paste0("Water and fuel collection on the diary day, by sex, age and sector", syn_note()), label = "burden",
    align = c("l", rep("r", 6)), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Survey-weighted means; FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. Any: share of persons with any minutes of fetching water (ICATUS 242) or gathering firewood and other natural fuel (241) on the diary day. Minutes: mean over all persons, including zeros. Minutes if collected: mean minutes of water and fuel collection together among persons with any. N: diaries.")
```

Table \ref{tab:burden} reports participation and minutes by sex, age group and sector. In rural areas, `r pct(pw_rw$est)` of women aged 18 and above fetched water on the diary day, against `r pct(pw_rm$est)` of men; the difference is `r diff_pp(g_pw)` for women. For fuel, the rates are `r pct(pf_rw$est)` and `r pct(pf_rm$est)`, a difference of `r ppx(g_pf)`. Averaged over all rural women, including those who did not collect, collection takes `r f1(mc_rw$est)` minutes a day, against `r f1(mc_rm$est)` minutes for men. Among those who collected, women spent `r f1(mcd_rw$est)` minutes and men `r f1(mcd_rm$est)` minutes. In urban areas, `r pct(pw_uw$est)` of women and `r pct(pw_um$est)` of men fetched water. Among rural adolescents aged 15 to 17, `r pct(pw_rg$est)` of girls and `r pct(pw_rb$est)` of boys fetched water, and among children aged 6 to 14, `r pct(pw_rg6$est)` of girls and `r pct(pw_rb6$est)` of boys.

```{r tab-share}
st <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Share of all collection minutes done by female members", "\\quad Rural", "\\quad Urban",
              "Share of water-fetching minutes done by female members", "Share of fuel-gathering minutes done by female members",
              "Share of all collection minutes done by girls under 18", "Share of all collection minutes done by children under 18",
              "Households in which any member collected", "\\quad Rural households",
              "Among them: only female members collected", "\\quad Rural", "\\quad Urban",
              "Among them: a girl under 18 collected"),
  Estimate = c(mcell(as.data.frame(sh_c), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(sh_c_r), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(sh_c_u), 100),
               mcell(as.data.frame(sh_w), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(sh_f), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(sh_girl), 100),
               mcell(as.data.frame(sh_child), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(hh_share_any), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(hh_share_any_r), 100),
               mcell(as.data.frame(hh_onlyf), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(hh_onlyf_r), 100), mcell(as.data.frame(hh_onlyf_u), 100),
               mcell(as.data.frame(hh_girl), 100)))
names(st) <- c("", "Per cent")
tab(st, caption = paste0("Concentration of collection on women and girls", syn_note()), label = "share",
    align = c("l", "r"), escape = FALSE,
    notes = "Minute shares: survey-weighted share of person-minutes of collection (ICATUS 241 and 242) done by the group, computed as a mean of the group indicator weighted by survey weight times minutes; FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. Household rows: households weighted by the mean survey weight of their diarists; only members aged six and above keep diaries, so collection by younger children is not observed.")
```

Table \ref{tab:share} shows how concentrated the work is. Female members do `r pct(sh_c$est)` of all minutes of water and fuel collection, `r pct(sh_w$est)` of water fetching and `r pct(sh_f$est)` of fuel gathering. `r iff(fem_major, "Collection is therefore predominantly women's and girls' work.", "Collection is therefore not predominantly done by female members in this sample.")` Girls under 18 do `r pct(sh_girl$est)` of all collection minutes. At the household level, `r pct(hh_share_any$est)` of households (`r pct(hh_share_any_r$est)` of rural households) had at least one member who collected on the diary day. Among them, `r pct(hh_onlyf$est)` relied only on female members (`r pct(hh_onlyf_r$est)` in rural and `r pct(hh_onlyf_u$est)` in urban areas), and in `r pct(hh_girl$est)` a girl under 18 was among those who collected. These household figures cover a single day and members aged six and above; a household whose members collect on other days of the week, or whose male members collect less often but in longer trips, is classified by the diary day only.

# Intrahousehold allocation {#sec:alloc}

## Women and men in the same household

To compare female and male members facing the same household needs, I estimate
$$ y_{ih} = \beta\, Female_{ih} + \alpha_{a(ih)} + \delta_{d(ih)} + \lambda_h + \varepsilon_{ih}, $$
for members $i$ aged 10 and above of household $h$, where $\alpha$ are age-band effects, $\delta$ are diary-day effects and $\lambda_h$ is a household fixed effect. The household fixed effect absorbs the household's water source, distance to it, cooking fuel, income, caste, location and the season of the survey. $\beta$ is the average difference between a female and a male member of the same household and age band. The sample is the `r fn(nrow(HB))` members of the `r fn(n_hh_B)` households with at least one female and one male member aged 10 and above.

```{r tab-hhfe}
ht <- data.frame(Outcome = b_y,
                 a = sapply(names(b_y), function(y) cell(kh(y), if (grepl("^any", y)) 100 else 1)),
                 b = sapply(names(b_y), function(y) cell(kh(y, mCS), if (grepl("^any", y)) 100 else 1)),
                 c = sapply(names(b_y), function(y) cell(kh(y, mHR, "female:urban"), if (grepl("^any", y)) 100 else 1)),
                 d = sapply(names(b_y), function(y) .fmt((if (grepl("^any", y)) 100 else 1) * wmean(HB[female == 0][[y]], HB[female == 0]$weight), 1)))
names(ht) <- c("Outcome", "Female, household FE", "Female, district FE", "Female x urban", "Male mean")
tab(ht, caption = paste0("Female minus male members aged 10 and above", syn_note()), label = "hhfe",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Household FE: household fixed effects, age-band and diary-day indicators. District FE: ", fe_words(fe_used(HB, FE_A)), " fixed effects, with age band, education, marital status, household size, members under six and aged 60 and above, and urban. Female x urban: interaction in the household FE model (the gap in urban households minus the gap in rural households). pp: percentage points. FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:hhfe} reports the results. Within households, female members spend `r diff_txt(k_hh)` on collection than male members of the same age band: `r diff_txt(k_hh_w)` fetching water and `r diff_txt(k_hh_f)` gathering fuel. Their probability of collecting on the diary day is `r diff_pp(k_hh_any)`. The cross-sectional estimate with district fixed effects is `r sg(k_cs)`. `r iff(ok(k_cs) && ok(k_hh) && abs(k_cs$est - k_hh$est) > 1.96 * k_hh$se, "The difference between the two shows that female and male members are not distributed evenly across households with different collection needs.", "The within-household and cross-sectional estimates are close, so the gap is not explained by female and male members living in different kinds of households.")` The gap in urban households differs from that in rural households by `r sg(k_hh_urb)`. `r iff(is_neg(k_hh_urb), "The gap is smaller in urban households, where fewer households collect at all.", "")`

## Position in the household

```{r tab-role}
roles_p <- roles[roles %in% role_means$role]          # positions held by at least one woman
rget <- function(r, v) { x <- role_means[role == r][[v]]; if (length(x)) x[1] else NA_real_ }
rt <- data.frame(Role = roles_p,
                 a = sapply(roles_p, function(r) cell(kr(mR0, r))),
                 b = sapply(roles_p, function(r) cell(kr(mR1, r))),
                 c = sapply(roles_p, function(r) cell(kr(mRa, r), 100)),
                 m = sapply(roles_p, function(r) .fmt(rget(r, "m"), 1)),
                 n = sapply(roles_p, function(r) fn(rget(r, "n"))))
rt <- rbind(rt, data.frame(Role = "Head's spouse (reference)", a = "", b = "", c = "",
                           m = .fmt(rget("Head's spouse", "m"), 1), n = fn(rget("Head's spouse", "n"))))
names(rt) <- c("Relative to head's spouse", "Minutes", "Minutes, age controls", "Any (pp), age controls", "Mean minutes", "N women")
tab(rt, caption = paste0("Collection by women's position in the household, women aged 15 and above", syn_note()), label = "role",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Household fixed effects; the sample is women aged 15 and above in the ", fn(uniqueN(WB$hh_id)), " households with women in at least two positions (", fn(nrow(WB)), " women). Age controls: age-band and diary-day indicators. Mean minutes and N: all women aged 15 and above in each position. Daughter: married or unmarried child of the head. FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:role} compares women in different positions in the same household, relative to the head's spouse. Without age controls, a daughter-in-law collects `r sg(k_dil0)` relative to the head's spouse and a daughter `r sg(k_dau0)`. With age controls, the estimates are `r sg(k_dil)` and `r sg(k_dau)`. The difference between a daughter-in-law and a daughter of the same age in the same household is `r sg(k_dil_dau)`; `r fn(n_hh_dil_dau)` households have both a daughter-in-law and a daughter aged 15 or above. `r iff(is_pos(k_dil_dau), "Daughters-in-law carry more of the household's collection than daughters, consistent with the weaker position of women who marry into the household.", iff(is_neg(k_dil_dau), "Daughters collect more than daughters-in-law of the same age, which suggests that unmarried daughters, who are often younger and have no children of their own, are assigned this work.", "The two do not differ significantly, so in these data the assignment of collection does not depend on whether a young woman was born into the household or married into it."))`

## Does another woman or a girl take the load off the main woman?

The third question is whether the presence of other members who could collect changes the collection time of the household's main married woman. The focal woman is a married woman aged 20 to 49 who is either the head or the head's spouse in a household with no daughter-in-law of childbearing age, or the only daughter-in-law of childbearing age; a woman at the head's level who lives with a married daughter-in-law is usually of the older generation and is excluded. There are `r fn(nrow(M))` such women. I regress her collection minutes, her participation and the collection minutes of all other diarists in her household on indicators for another non-employed woman aged 18 to 69 (whose usual status is not employment, education or disability), a girl aged 10 to 17 and a boy aged 10 to 17, controlling for her age and education, sector, the number of men aged 18 and above, the number of other employed women, the numbers of members under six, aged 6 to 14 and aged 60 and above, and proxy reporting, with `r fe_words(fe_used(M, FE_A))` fixed effects. Comparing the girl coefficient with the boy coefficient holds constant the arrival of an adolescent and isolates the role of the adolescent's sex.

```{r tab-mother}
mt <- data.frame(Term = c("Another non-employed woman 18--69", "Girl aged 10--17 present", "Boy aged 10--17 present", "Girl minus boy"),
                 sapply(names(mo_y), function(y) {
                   s <- if (y == "any_collect") 100 else 1; m <- mMo[[y]]
                   c(cell(coef_of(m, "oth_nonemp"), s), cell(coef_of(m, "girl1017"), s), cell(coef_of(m, "boy1017"), s),
                     cell(lin2(m, "girl1017", "boy1017", -1), s))
                 }),
                 r = c(cell(k_mo_w_r), cell(k_mo_g_r), cell(coef_of(mMoR, "boy1017")), cell(lin2(mMoR, "girl1017", "boy1017", -1))),
                 check.names = FALSE)
names(mt) <- c("", mo_y, "Her minutes, rural")
tab(mt, caption = paste0("The main married woman's collection and the presence of other potential collectors", syn_note()), label = "mother",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Married women aged 20--49 who are the head or head's spouse (no daughter-in-law of childbearing age present) or the only daughter-in-law (N = ", fn(nrow(M)), "; rural N = ", fn(nrow(M[rural == 1])), "). Others' collection: minutes of all other diarists in the household. Controls listed in the text. pp: percentage points. FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:mother} reports the estimates. The main married woman collects `r f1(mean_M)` minutes a day on average. When another non-employed adult woman lives in the household, her own collection differs by `r sg(k_mo_w)`, and other members' collection by `r sg(k_mo_w_oth)`. When an adolescent girl is present, her collection differs by `r sg(k_mo_g)`, and the difference between the girl and the boy coefficients is `r sg(k_mo_gb)`. `r iff(is_neg(k_mo_gb), "Adolescent daughters, but not sons, take part of the collection load off the main woman.", iff(is_neg(k_mo_g), "The main woman collects less when an adolescent girl is present, but the difference from an adolescent boy is not significant, so the data do not isolate a role of the adolescent's sex.", "The presence of an adolescent girl is not associated with significantly less collection by the main woman."))` `r iff(is_neg(k_mo_w), "Another non-employed adult woman is associated with less collection by the main woman, consistent with a sharing of the work among adult women.", "Another non-employed adult woman is not associated with significantly less collection by the main woman.")` `r iff(is_pos(k_mo_g_oth), "Other members' collection is higher when an adolescent girl is present, which is what one would expect if the girl does part of it.", "")` These comparisons are across households, with district fixed effects; households with and without an adolescent girl or another adult woman differ in other ways, including in their stage of the life cycle, so I read them as descriptive of how the burden is shared rather than as the causal effect of adding a member.

# Seasonal collection need and what it displaces {#sec:season}

## Design

Collection need varies over the year. In the dry months before the monsoon, nearby wells, ponds and hand pumps run low, and water must be carried from further away or waited for; fuel gathering also has seasonal patterns linked to the agricultural calendar and to the availability of crop residues. Because the survey allotted equal numbers of first-stage units to each sub-round, households in the same district were surveyed in different quarters. Comparing collection across quarters within a district therefore estimates how collection varies with the season, holding the district fixed.

I use this in two ways. The first is a reduced form for rural persons:
$$ y_{ij} = \pi\, Q2_{j} + X_{ij}'\gamma + \delta_{d(j)} + \omega_{w(ij)} + u_{ij}, $$
where $Q2_j$ indicates that first-stage unit $j$ was surveyed in sub-round 2, $\delta_{d}$ are district fixed effects, $\omega$ diary-day effects and $X$ age band, education, marital status, household size and the numbers of members under six and aged 60 and above. Estimated for each of the ten categories of the day, the coefficients $\pi$ sum to zero by the 1,440-minute identity, so the reduced form shows where extra collection time comes from.

The second is a two-stage least squares estimate [@angrist2009mostly] of the minutes of each other activity per minute of collection, on rural and urban persons together. Collection minutes are instrumented by the interactions of the three later sub-rounds with rural residence, with district-by-sector fixed effects and sub-round fixed effects:
$$ y_{ij} = \theta\, C_{ij} + X_{ij}'\gamma + \delta_{d(j),s(j)} + \tau_{q(j)} + \omega_{w(ij)} + u_{ij}, \qquad C_{ij} = \sum_{q=2}^{4} \phi_q\, \mathbf{1}[q(j) = q]\times Rural_j + \ldots $$
The sub-round fixed effects $\tau_q$ absorb everything about the quarter that is common to rural and urban areas, such as festivals, school calendars, heat and national events. What remains is the extra seasonal variation in rural areas, where collection is common, relative to urban areas in the same quarter. Because the ten categories partition the day, the nine coefficients $\theta$ for the activities other than collection sum to minus one.

## Threats

Sub-round is a shifter of collection need, not a randomised instrument, and the exclusion restriction (that the rural quarter affects other activities only through collection) is strong. The main threat is agriculture. The rural quarter also moves the demand for agricultural labour: sowing, weeding and harvest fall in particular months, so paid work and own-account farming vary with the season for reasons unrelated to collection. If the high-need quarter for water is also a slack or peak agricultural season, the reduced form for paid work mixes the two. Other threats are seasonal illness, the timing of festivals and weddings that differs between rural and urban areas, and school calendars that differ by sector. I address the agricultural threat in four ways: by testing whether paid work moves with the rural quarter for men, whose collection is low; by controlling for usual principal activity status; by dropping agricultural workers; and by restricting the sample to women who are not employed. I also add state-by-quarter fixed effects, which absorb seasonal shocks common to rural and urban areas of a state. None of these makes the quarter random, and I interpret the two-stage estimates as the time cost of seasonal collection need under the assumption that the remaining seasonal variation operates through collection.

## Collection across quarters

```{r fig-quarter, fig.cap = paste0("Collection minutes by sub-round, rural, relative to sub-round 1", syn_note()), fig.height = 3.1}

if (nrow(pq)) {
  pq[, group := factor(gsub("--", "-", group), levels = gsub("--", "-", names(prof_grp)))]
  ggplot(pq, aes(factor(q), est, colour = group)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = est - 1.96 * se, ymax = est + 1.96 * se), position = position_dodge(0.4), size = 0.3) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Women 15+" = "#C2512F", "Men 15+" = "#2C6E9B", "Girls 10-17" = "#E0A030"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Sub-round", y = "Minutes per day (vs sub-round 1)",

} else {
```
