```{r fig-quarter, fig.cap = paste0("Collection minutes by sub-round, rural, relative to sub-round 1", syn_note()), fig.height = 3.1}
}
```

Figure \ref{fig:fig-quarter} plots collection minutes in each sub-round relative to the first, within districts, for rural women, men and girls. `r iff(!is.na(peak_q), paste0("Rural women's mean collection is highest in sub-round ", peak_q, "."), "")` `r iff(isTRUE(peak_q == 2), "This is the quarter designated in advance as the period of highest need.", iff(!is.na(peak_q), "This is not the quarter designated as the period of highest need, so the designation of sub-round 2 is not borne out by the data and the reduced form below should be read with that in mind.", ""))`

## Reduced form

```{r tab-rf}
rft <- data.frame(Activity = RA,
                  w = sapply(names(RA), function(y) cell(krf(RFw, y))),
                  m = sapply(names(RA), function(y) cell(krf(RFm, y))),
                  g = sapply(names(RA), function(y) cell(krf(RFg, y))))
rft <- rbind(rft, data.frame(Activity = "Sum of the ten coefficients",
                             w = f2(rf_sum_w), m = f2(sum(sapply(names(RA), function(y) krf(RFm, y)$est), na.rm = TRUE)),
                             g = f2(sum(sapply(names(RA), function(y) krf(RFg, y)$est), na.rm = TRUE))))
rft <- rbind(rft, data.frame(Activity = "N", w = fn(nrow(A15r[female == 1])), m = fn(nrow(A15r[female == 0])), g = fn(nrow(G[rural == 1]))))
names(rft) <- c("Minutes per day", "Women 15+", "Men 15+", "Girls 10--17")
tab(rft, caption = paste0("Reduced form: sub-round 2 versus other quarters, rural, within district", syn_note()), label = "rf",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Each cell is the coefficient on an indicator for sub-round 2 from a regression with ", fe_words(fe_used(A15r, FE_R)), " fixed effects and controls for age band, education, marital status, household size and members under six and aged 60 and above (girls: single-year age, head's education, household size, members under six and 60 and above). The ten categories partition the day, so the coefficients sum to zero. FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:rf} reports the reduced form. Rural women's collection in sub-round 2 is `r diff_txt(rf_w, "higher", "lower")` than in the other quarters of the same district, from a base of `r f1(base_rw)` minutes in the other quarters. For men it is `r diff_txt(rf_m, "higher", "lower")`, and for girls aged 10 to 17 `r diff_txt(rf_g, "higher", "lower")`. `r iff(rf_up_w && !rf_up_m, "Seasonal collection need falls on women, not on men.", iff(rf_up_w && rf_up_m, "Both women's and men's collection rise in the high-need quarter.", "Collection is not significantly higher in sub-round 2 for women."))` Women's paid work in the same quarter differs by `r sg(rf_w_emp)` and men's by `r sg(rf_m_emp)`. `r iff(abs(rf_sum_w) < 0.005, "The ten coefficients for women sum to zero to two decimal places, as the identity requires.", paste0("The ten coefficients for women sum to ", f2(rf_sum_w), " minutes."))`

## Two-stage estimates

```{r tab-iv}
ivt <- data.frame(Activity = RA[DISP],
                  w = sapply(DISP, function(y) cell(kiv(IVw, y), 1, 2)),
                  m = sapply(DISP, function(y) cell(kiv(IVm, y), 1, 2)),
                  g = sapply(DISP, function(y) cell(kiv(IVg, y), 1, 2)))
ivt <- rbind(ivt, data.frame(Activity = c("Sum of the nine coefficients", "First-stage F (cluster-robust)", "N"),
                             w = c(f2(ivs_w), f1(F_w), fn(if (is.null(IVw$employment)) NA else nobs(IVw$employment))),
                             m = c(f2(ivs_m), f1(F_m), fn(if (is.null(IVm$employment)) NA else nobs(IVm$employment))),
                             g = c(f2(iv_sum(IVg)), f1(F_g), fn(if (is.null(IVg$learning)) NA else nobs(IVg$learning)))))
names(ivt) <- c("Minutes per minute of collection", "Women 15+", "Men 15+", "Girls 10--17")
tab(ivt, caption = paste0("Two-stage least squares: other activities per minute of water and fuel collection", syn_note()), label = "iv",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Collection minutes instrumented by sub-round 2, 3 and 4 interacted with rural residence. ", cap1(fe_words(fe_used(A15, FE_IV))), " fixed effects; controls as in the reduced form. Rural and urban persons. The nine coefficients sum to minus one by the 1,440-minute identity. First-stage F: cluster-robust Wald statistic for the three excluded instruments. FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:iv} reports the two-stage estimates. The first-stage F statistic for women is `r f1(F_w)`, `r f1(F_m)` for men and `r f1(F_g)` for girls. `r iff(strong_w, iff(lmmp_w, "For women it exceeds both the conventional threshold of 10 and the higher threshold that @lee2022valid show is needed for conventional t-ratio inference at the 5 per cent level.", paste0("For women it exceeds the conventional threshold of 10 [@stock2005testing], but not the threshold of 104.7 that @lee2022valid show is needed for conventional t-ratios to have correct size at the 5 per cent level, so the confidence intervals below should be read as approximate.")), "For women it is below the conventional threshold of 10 [@stock2005testing; @andrews2019weak], so the instruments are weak and the two-stage estimates are biased towards the ordinary least squares estimates and unreliable for inference. I report them for completeness and base conclusions on the reduced form.")` In sub-round 2, rural women's collection rises by `r sg(fs_w)` relative to urban women in the same district and quarter, compared with sub-round 1 (first stage).

`r iff(strong_w && !is.na(top_disp_w), paste0("For women, the most negative coefficient, and so the point estimate of the largest offsetting change, is for ", tolower(RA[top_disp_w]), ": each additional minute of collection is associated with a change of ", cse(kiv(IVw, top_disp_w)), " minutes. The next is ", tolower(RA[top2_disp_w]), ", with ", cse(kiv(IVw, top2_disp_w)), " minutes."), "Because the first stage for women is weak, I do not interpret the individual two-stage coefficients.")` The coefficients for paid work, unpaid domestic services, free time and sleep are `r cse(k_iv_w_emp)`, `r cse(k_iv_w_dom)`, `r cse(k_iv_w_free)` and `r cse(k_iv_w_sleep)`. `r iff(!strong_m, "Men's collection responds too little to the rural quarter for their two-stage estimates to be informative.", "")` `r iff(strong_w && is_neg(k_iv_w_emp), "Seasonal collection need is associated with less paid work by women, which is the margin on which water infrastructure has been expected to raise women's earnings [@ilahi2000public; @koolwal2013access].", iff(strong_w, "Women's paid work does not fall significantly with collection, which is consistent with the evidence of @koolwal2013access that time saved from water collection does not necessarily go to paid work.", ""))` `r iff(strong_w && (is_neg(k_iv_w_free) || is_neg(k_iv_w_sleep)), "Part of the time comes out of free time or sleep, which, as @devoto2012happiness emphasise, are where the gains from easier access to water may be largest in welfare terms.", "")` For girls aged 10 to 17, the learning coefficient is `r cse(k_iv_g_learn)` minutes per minute of collection, and the free-time coefficient `r cse(k_iv_g_free)`. `r iff(strong_g && is_neg(k_iv_g_learn), "Girls' extra collection in the high-need season comes partly out of learning.", iff(strong_g, "Girls' learning time does not fall significantly with seasonal collection.", "The first stage for girls is weak, so these estimates are not informative."))`

## Agricultural seasonality and robustness

The reduced form for men's paid work, with the same fixed effects as the two-stage estimate, gives a joint p-value of `r f2(thr_m$p)` for the three quarter-by-rural interactions; for women the p-value is `r f2(thr_w$p)`. `r iff(paid_seasonal, "Paid work therefore varies with the rural quarter. Because men's collection is low, the variation in men's paid work is unlikely to be caused by collection, and it points to agricultural seasonality that may also move women's paid work directly. The two-stage coefficient for women's paid work should therefore not be read as the effect of collection alone.", "Paid work does not vary significantly with the rural quarter, for men or for women. This does not rule out agricultural seasonality in other activities, but it removes the most obvious violation of the exclusion restriction.")`

```{r tab-robust}
rbt <- data.frame(Specification = sapply(specs, `[[`, "lab"),
                  t(sapply(names(specs), function(s) sapply(rb_y, function(y) cell(RB[[s]]$k[[y]], 1, 2)))),
                  F = sapply(names(specs), function(s) f1(RB[[s]]$F)),
                  N = sapply(names(specs), function(s) fn(RB[[s]]$n)), check.names = FALSE)
names(rbt) <- c("Specification", "Employment", "Unpaid domestic", "Free time", "Sleep", "First-stage F", "N")
tab(rbt, caption = paste0("Robustness of women's two-stage estimates (minutes per minute of collection)", syn_note()), label = "robust",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = "Women aged 15 and above. Each row re-estimates the baseline two-stage model for women on the sample or with the controls shown. Agricultural workers: usual status employed and NIC 2008 division 01--03. State-by-quarter fixed effects replace the sub-round fixed effects. Self-reported: diaries reported by the woman herself. -- : not estimable. FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.")
```

Table \ref{tab:robust} reports the checks for women. Controlling for usual principal activity status, the paid-work coefficient is `r cse(rb_emp_pas)`. `r iff(ok(rb_emp_noag), paste0("Excluding agricultural workers, it is ", cse(rb_emp_noag), "."), "The check that excludes agricultural workers is not estimable because the industry code is not available.")` `r iff(ok(rb_emp_nemp), paste0("Among women who are not employed in their usual status, it is ", cse(rb_emp_nemp), "."), "Among women who are not employed in their usual status, paid work on the diary day does not vary enough to estimate the paid-work coefficient.")` Of the `r n_rb_est` alternative specifications that can be estimated, `r n_rb_same_emp` give a paid-work coefficient with the same sign as the baseline. `r iff(n_rb_est > 0 && n_rb_same_emp == n_rb_est, "The sign of the paid-work estimate is stable across the checks.", "The sign of the paid-work estimate is not stable across all checks, so the paid-work margin is not robustly identified.")`

# Girls' collection and learning {#sec:girls}

```{r tab-sib}
sbt <- data.frame(Outcome = sib_y,
                  a = sapply(names(sib_y), function(y) cell(coef_of(mS[[y]], "girl"), if (y == "any_collect") 100 else 1)),
                  b = sapply(names(sib_y), function(y) cell(coef_of(mSq[[y]], "girl:hi"), if (y == "any_collect") 100 else 1)),
                  c = sapply(names(sib_y), function(y) cell(coef_of(mSr[[y]], "girl:rural"), if (y == "any_collect") 100 else 1)),
                  d = sapply(names(sib_y), function(y) .fmt((if (y == "any_collect") 100 else 1) * wmean(S[girl == 0][[y]], S[girl == 0]$weight), 1)))
names(sbt) <- c("Outcome", "Girl", "Girl x sub-round 2", "Girl x rural", "Boys' mean")
tab(sbt, caption = paste0("Sisters and brothers aged 10--17: girl minus boy, minutes per day", syn_note()), label = "sib",
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Sibling-set fixed effects and single-year age effects; never-married children or grandchildren of the head aged 10--17 in ", fn(n_sets), " mixed-sex sets (", fn(nrow(S)), " children). Each interaction column is a separate regression adding girl x the set-level indicator. pp: percentage points. FSU-clustered standard errors in parentheses. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

The last question is whether collection competes with girls' schooling. Table \ref{tab:sib} compares sisters and brothers aged 10 to 17 in the same sibling set, with single-year age effects, so that the household's water source and needs are held fixed. Girls spend `r diff_txt(k_s_c)` collecting than their brothers, and their probability of collecting on the diary day is `r diff_pp(k_s_a)`. Their learning time differs by `r sg(k_s_l)`. In sub-round 2, the girl-boy gap in collection changes by `r sg(k_s_cq)` and the gap in learning by `r sg(k_s_lq)`. `r iff(is_pos(k_s_cq) && is_neg(k_s_lq), "In the high-need quarter, girls' extra collection rises and their learning time falls relative to their brothers', which is the pattern expected if collection competes with schooling.", iff(is_pos(k_s_cq), "In the high-need quarter, girls' extra collection rises relative to their brothers', but the learning gap does not widen significantly.", "The girl-boy gap in collection does not rise significantly in the high-need quarter."))` These comparisons are short by design. Sibling comparisons of children's time raise selection issues created by son-biased fertility, which I do not address here.

# Discussion {#sec:disc}

## Interpretation

`r iff(fem_major, "Water and fuel collection in India is overwhelmingly the work of women and girls.", "Water and fuel collection in India is shared between women and men to a greater degree than the literature suggests.")` The household fixed-effects estimates show that this is not because women and men live in different households: within the same household, facing the same source and the same need, female members do `r iff(is_pos(k_hh), "more", "no significantly different amount")` of the work. `r iff(is_pos(k_dil_dau), "The extra burden on daughters-in-law points to position in the household, and not only sex and age, as a determinant of who collects.", "")` `r iff(is_neg(k_mo_gb), "That adolescent girls, but not boys, take part of the burden off the main woman shows how the division of collection is passed from one generation of women to the next.", "")`

The seasonal estimates add a time-cost dimension. `r iff(rf_up_w, "When collection need rises in the high-need quarter, women's collection rises and other activities must fall to make room for it.", "Collection does not rise significantly in the quarter designated as the high-need season, so the seasonal design does not identify a time cost.")` `r iff(rf_up_w && strong_w && !is.na(top_disp_w), paste0("The point estimate of the largest offsetting change for women is in ", tolower(RA[top_disp_w]), "."), "")` `r iff(paid_seasonal, "Because paid work also moves with the rural quarter, I cannot separate the time cost of collection from agricultural seasonality on the paid-work margin.", "")` These estimates describe the response to seasonal increases in need; the response to a permanent reduction in collection time, such as a household tap connection, may differ, because households adjust slowly and because time released permanently can be committed to activities, such as a regular job, that a seasonal fluctuation cannot.

## Policy

The Jal Jeevan Mission aims to provide every rural household with a functional tap connection [@mojs2019jjm]. The estimates here bear on the benefits of that programme in three ways. First, they quantify the time now spent on water collection and show who spends it. Second, they show that collection need varies seasonally, so a connection that delivers water reliably in the dry season saves more time than an average day suggests, and one that fails in the dry season saves less. Third, the reallocation estimates show which activities absorb seasonal increases in collection. `r iff(strong_w && (is_neg(k_iv_w_free) || is_neg(k_iv_w_sleep)), "To the extent that collection displaces rest and free time, the welfare gains from water connections are partly gains in rest and free time, which do not appear in labour statistics.", "")` Fuel gathering remains common despite the expansion of LPG [@kar2019ujjwala; @gould2018lpg], and the same diaries can track whether it falls as clean cooking spreads. The survey can be repeated, so the gender gap in collection time is a natural indicator for monitoring both programmes.

## Limitations

Five limitations matter. First, the unit-level file has no household questionnaire, so I observe neither the household's drinking water source nor its cooking fuel. The household fixed effects absorb these within households, but the descriptive and seasonal analyses cannot distinguish households that collect because they lack a connection from households that have one that does not work. Second, each person reports one day. Collection that happens every few days, such as weekly fuel trips, is measured accurately on average but not for an individual, and the household share in which only female members collected is a diary-day measure. Third, travel related to own-use production has its own code, so collection minutes understate the time cost if part of the walking is recorded as travel. Fourth, children under six keep no diary, and the roster does not identify parents, so mothers and their children are matched by relationship to the head and age. Fifth, the seasonal design rests on the assumption that the rural quarter affects other activities only through collection, which agricultural seasonality may violate; the months of each sub-round are not stated in the 2024 dictionary, and I take them from the 2019 design. The file records no caste or social group, religion or consumption expenditure, so I cannot show how the burden varies along these dimensions, and the cross-household comparisons control for socioeconomic status only through education, regular employment and district fixed effects.

# Conclusion {#sec:conc}

Full-day diaries for every household member show who carries water and fuel in India. In rural areas, `r pct(pw_rw$est)` of adult women and `r pct(pw_rm$est)` of adult men fetched water on the diary day, and female members do `r pct(sh_c$est)` of all collection minutes. Within the same household, female members aged 10 and above spend `r diff_txt(k_hh)` collecting than male members. `r iff(rf_up_w, paste0("In the quarter of highest expected need, rural women's collection is ", diff_txt(rf_w, "higher", "lower"), " than in other quarters of the same district."), "Collection does not rise significantly in the quarter designated as the period of highest need.")` `r iff(strong_w && !is.na(top_disp_w), paste0("The point estimate of the largest offsetting change is in ", tolower(RA[top_disp_w]), "."), "")` The gender gap in collection time is measurable in any time-use survey and is a direct indicator of the benefits that water and clean-fuel programmes can deliver to women and girls.
